title: Memory Allocation Simulator for Continuous Batching & KV/Activation Balancing
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Build a reproducible simulator that models GPU memory budgets across three primary consumers (model weights, KV cache, activations) under continuous batching. The simulator will evaluate different headroom reservation strategies and eviction policies to produce actionable memory allocations and SLO-aware knobs for the serving runtime.
background: We routinely hit out-of-memory (OOM) scenarios in mixed workloads where long-context KV-heavy requests coexist with short, latency-sensitive requests. Existing telemetry gives per-request HWM but lacks a forward-looking allocation policy that considers continuous batching dynamics (batch window, packing efficiency), KV shard locality, and activation transient peaks. This ticket scopes a simulator to quantify trade-offs and generate conservative reserve rules for per-GPU headroom and eviction thresholds.
goals: 1) Quantify memory headroom required to keep P99 latency degradation under configured SLOs for representative mixes. 2) Produce a small set of policy recommendations (static reserve percentage, dynamic slack algorithm, per-tenant caps) for runtime engineers. 3) Validate proposed policies against historical traces and a synthetic stress suite.
approach:
- Ingest traces: recent 30-day serving traces (sampling at 1% for long traces), synthetic traces for extreme tails.
- Model components: weights (static), KV cache (persistent per-session shards with LRU/time-decay), activations (ephemeral per-batch peak).
- Continuous batching model: simulate packing with parameters: target_latency_ms, max_batch_wait_ms, max_batch_size_tokens, packing efficiency (tokens-to-weight multiplier).
- Headroom strategies to evaluate: fixed-percent reserve, moving-average reserve (EWMA over recent high-water-marks), token-aware reserve (weighted by expected activation growth), and emergency preemption (drop lower-priority requests when predicted HWM > capacity).
- Eviction policies: global LRU across tenants, per-tenant soft caps with background compaction, KV-shard probabilistic eviction (favor oldest shards), and activation spill-to-host (simulated slow-path).
technical_details:
- Units: all memory in MiB.
- Memory budget equation per-GPU: Available = GPU_total - reserved_system - reserve_headroom. Peak_required = weights + max(KV_sum_current, KV_sum_after_prefetch) + activation_peak.
- Activation model: activation_peak = sum_over_requests(batch_size_tokens * tokens_to_activation_coef * model_activation_multiplier).
- KV growth: model per-session average growth rate (KB/token) and TTL-based decay.
- Packing latency trade-off: simulate N parallel packers; packing increases activation concurrency which raises peak transient memory.
- Outputs: HWM distribution percentiles, eviction counts by policy, predicted P50/P95/P99 latencies, fractional utilizations of weights/KV/activations, frequency of emergency preemption events.
- Implementation: Python-based discrete-event simulator using SimPy for concurrency + pandas for trace transforms + optional Rust core later if performance needed.
- Configurable knobs via YAML experiments file to sweep target_latency_ms, batch_wait_ms, reserve_pct, kv_ttl_seconds, per_tenant_cap_mb.
metrics:
- Memory overflow rate (OOMs per 1M requests).
- P99 latency regression (absolute ms and % over SLO).
- Average token cost delta (simulated cost impact from higher reserve).
- KV eviction frequency and average lifetime of shards.
- Simulated throughput loss under each policy (requests/sec).
experiment_plan:
1) Baseline run on 30-day sampled traces with current conservative 12% fixed reserve. 2) Sweep reserve_pct in [4,8,12,20] and observe OOM+latency. 3) Evaluate moving-average reserve with EWMA alpha in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]. 4) Test token-aware reserve where reserve = base_pct + k * recent_token_rate. 5) Simulate emergency preemption with priority tiers to measure latency impact on tiered workloads. 6) Run stress scenarios: KV growth storm (all sessions append), bursty long-context storms, and mixed small-high throughput.
Expected timeline: sim infra & ingestion (2 weeks), run experiments (2 weeks), analyze & produce recommendations (1 week).
rollout_plan:
- Deliver simulator and baseline report to runtime team for review.
- Pilot dynamic reserve on a small Dedicated fleet (5 GPUs across 2 clusters) with telemetry and kill-switch.
- Monitor for 2 weeks: key metrics OOM rate and P99 latency.
- If stable, roll to more fleets and codify policy as runtime default with feature flag.
- Document in Console: per-route memory forecast and recommended route-level caps.
acceptance_criteria: Simulator reproduces historical HWM percentiles within +/-10% for sampled traces.
Produce at least three distinct policy recommendations with quantified trade-offs (OOM rate vs token-cost vs P99 latency).
Runbook entry for emergency preemption behavior and safe rollback steps written and reviewed by SRE.
Pilot config (YAML) that can be deployed behind a runtime feature flag and tested on Dedicated without code changes to serving runtime.
Performance: simulator can run end-to-end experiment sweep on sampled 30-day traces within 24 hours on a build machine (CI runner).
testing_steps: Unit tests for memory accounting math (weights + KV + activations).
Integration test: ingest one-day trace X and assert HWM distribution shape matches stored telemetry snapshot within tolerance.
Smoke test: run stress scenario and ensure simulator reports an OOM when deliberately lowering reserve below physical requirement.
E2E: export policy YAML and use runtime feature flag to compare predicted vs actual memory headroom on pilot GPUs.
Chaos test: randomize packing efficiency and KV growth parameters to validate policy robustness.
implementation_notes:
- Start with a library that shares parsing code with telemetry ingestion used by observability team.
- Keep simulator pure (no RPCs to runtime); produce artifacts (CSV/JSON) consumed by dashboards.
- Use type-annotated Python and contract tests for model coefficients.
- Consider a follow-up ticket to upstream the eviction policy to C++ serving runtime if a clear winner emerges.
